operations.evidence: ONS publishes police recorded crime statistics quarterly; the Home Office collates data from 43 territorial police forces and British Transport Police; the Home Office supplies the collated data to ONS.
the production chain does not make force-level recording practices uniform; quarterly publication is not parcel-level evidence.
police recorded crime is published as official statistics; its National Statistics designation was removed in 2014; quality and consistency concerns motivated the removal.
official-statistics status is not the same as accredited official statistics; designation applies to the statistical series rather than every operational record.

the quality review examined how Home Office Counting Rules are interpreted; the review examined how the rules are applied by police forces; rule interpretation is a potential source of quality variation.
a national rule does not prove identical force implementation; recording-rule compliance is not a parcel safety measure.
OSR examined the IT systems police forces use to record crime; system strengths and limitations can affect data quality; the review treated technology as part of the end-to-end quality process.
IT-system differences do not by themselves quantify bias; system quality must not be inferred from a force-level total.
the review examined quality assurance by police-force analysts; it also examined Home Office quality assurance; ONS quality assurance formed a third level of review.
quality assurance at one level does not replace controls at another; QA processes do not prove that every record is correct.
the Home Office runs a monthly quality-assurance process; the monthly process includes logic checks; the monthly process includes consistency checks.
monthly checks can detect defined anomalies but not every root cause; passing checks is not equivalent to spatial validation.

the Home Office conducts a more detailed quarterly reconciliation; the reconciliation supports data sent to ONS for publication; the quarterly process contains further checks beyond the monthly process.
quarterly reconciliation is publication QA rather than real-time validation; reconciliation cannot be treated as a local crime-rate denominator.
OSR found that Home Office quality-assurance processes are well established; the Home Office Data Hub strengthened assurance arrangements; quality processes have improved in recent years.
strengthened assurance does not remove all force-level quality issues; process maturity is not a numerical safety score.
OSR said the Home Office should strengthen oversight of police-force data quality; gaps remain in understanding force-level quality; published quality information is incomplete.
an oversight gap does not identify the direction or size of error for a particular force; missing quality information must not be replaced with inferred values.

OSR found that both ONS and the Home Office strengthened quality arrangements; OSR also found gaps in their understanding of police-force data quality; communication of quality improved but remained incomplete.
improved communication does not make non-comparable series directly comparable; quality gaps require explicit caveats.
OSR recommended a joint ONS and Home Office action plan; the plan was intended to address review recommendations; the recommendations were described as critical before reassessment against the Code.
an action plan is not evidence that every recommendation is complete; reassessment status must be checked separately.
OSR organised recommendations into three improvement areas; the framework covers data-quality oversight and statistical communication; the framework supports future reassessment.
framework structure is not a force ranking; recommendation coverage does not supply parcel-level outcomes.
OSR recognised substantial progress in crime recording; OSR also identified remaining challenges and oversight gaps; further Home Office and ONS action was requested.
progress since 2014 does not establish uniform current quality; remaining challenges must stay visible in trend interpretation.
police recorded crime measures crimes reported to and recorded by police; the data can indicate police workload; the series can be reliable for trends in some crime types.
workload is not the same construct as victimisation prevalence; fitness for trend analysis is offence-specific.
OSR gathered evidence from police forces; HMICFRS was included among stakeholders; ONS and Home Office statisticians also contributed.
stakeholder consultation is not an independent record-level audit; different stakeholders can hold different quality information.

ONS adjusted both CSEW and police recorded crime series to form comparable subsets; coverage differences prevent direct use of the full series; the comparison focused on offence types covered by both sources.
the comparable subset is not the complete crime total; adjustments do not make the collection methods identical.
both comparable series declined from year ending March 2003 to year ending March 2014; CSEW comparable incidents fell over the period; police recorded comparable offences also fell.
national historical movement is not a parcel-level trajectory; the comparison uses constructed comparable subsets.

the CSEW comparable series generally continued to decrease; police recorded comparable offences rose between year ending March 2015 and March 2019; ONS linked much of the rise to improved recording practices.
recording improvements can increase recorded volumes without equal growth in victimisation; the finding does not exclude genuine change.
the National Crime Recording Standard was introduced in April 2002; ONS begins the comparable analysis at year ending March 2003; the standard aimed to improve consistency in police recording.
the standard does not guarantee perfect consistency; pre- and post-standard data require methodological context.
ONS noted the possibility that some forces may over-record crime in some way; the potential scale was described as small; ONS judged it likely to have minimal impact on the ratio disparity.
possible over-recording must not be assigned to a force without evidence; minimal aggregate impact does not validate individual records.
police recorded crime is the primary source of local crime statistics; it is useful for offences that are well reported to police; it is useful where police recording is reliable.
local usefulness is offence-specific; the source misses unreported and unrecorded offences.
